narrative.headline: Sindarov leaves theory with a thoughtful a3
narrative.text: Sindarov spent 7 minutes on 14.a3, a novelty that took the game out of known theory, and the engine rated it a good move. The engine slightly preferred Be3, a line that leads to a queen trade, while a3 is a quiet pawn move that commits the pawn structure. One likely reason for the think is that this was the first move without book guidance, so Sindarov probably had to work things out alone for the first time. With at least 5 good moves available and a low difficulty rating, the choice was more about picking a direction than avoiding a trap. Gukesh had just played 13...Qb8 in only 6 seconds, which suggests Gukesh was still in preparation, while Sindarov was already about 33 minutes behind on the clock. After the move Sindarov had 1h 18m left against Gukesh's 1h 58m.

likely_reasons.reason: Sindarov was the one leaving theory with a novelty, so 14.a3 was probably the first move Sindarov had to calculate independently.
With at least 5 good options, including a Be3 line that trades queens and pawn moves like a3 or c3 that commit the structure, Sindarov may have spent time choosing what kind of middlegame to play.
Gukesh's near-instant 13...Qb8 hinted that Gukesh was still in home preparation, which may have made Sindarov extra careful despite already trailing on the clock.

narrative.headline: Gukesh finds the only good queen capture
narrative.text: Gukesh spent 11 minutes before playing 16...Qxd4, which the engine rates as the best move and the only good option in the position. The engine's evaluation barely moved, from -0.1 to -0.11 pawns, so the game stayed roughly balanced. The alternatives were clearly worse: the other queen capture, Qxc2, dropped to -0.57 pawns, and the pawn move c5 would have committed the structure at -1.57. Sindarov had just spent over 15 minutes on 16.b3, and the game was only two moves out of known theory after Sindarov's 14.a3, so Gukesh was probably calculating fresh positions on Gukesh's own. This was Gukesh's first think of over 10 minutes in the game, and with a big clock lead (1h 57m before, 1h 46m after, against Sindarov's 1h 03m) Gukesh could probably afford to make sure.

likely_reasons.reason: Only one move kept the balance, and a similar-looking queen capture, Qxc2, was noticeably worse, so Gukesh probably needed to check carefully.
The game had just left theory after Sindarov's 14.a3, and Sindarov's long-considered 16.b3 may have given Gukesh new ideas to work through.
A comfortable clock lead of nearly an hour probably let Gukesh invest time without worry.

narrative.headline: Gukesh spends nearly sixteen minutes on gxf4
narrative.text: Sindarov played the pawn push 29.f4 after only 25 seconds, and Gukesh answered with the capture 29...gxf4, which the engine also rates as its top choice, keeping the game balanced at roughly 0.0. It was Gukesh's longest think of the game, 15 minutes 51 seconds, cutting Gukesh's clock from 35m 32s to 19m 41s against Sindarov's 12m 47s. One likely reason is that every serious option, whether gxf4, c5 or g4, would permanently change the pawn structure in an endgame where such decisions are hard to undo. The engine counted 4 good moves, so Gukesh probably had to weigh several reasonable paths, even though the alternatives c5 and g4 were only slightly worse at -0.24. The game was also 15 moves past known theory after Sindarov's 14.a3, and Gukesh had already invested more than ten minutes on four earlier moves, suggesting a careful, calculation-heavy approach throughout.

narrative.headline: Sindarov finds the only move to hold
narrative.text: In the endgame, Sindarov played 49.Bxe1, the engine's top choice, keeping the position level at about 0.00. It was an only-move situation: the engine saw just one good move, with alternatives like f7 (-6.93) and Kh4 (-8.93) losing badly. Gukesh had just played 48...Kxf5, a king capture that probably demanded an accurate reply. The engine rated the difficulty at the maximum, yet Sindarov spent only 49 seconds, roughly matching Gukesh's 50-second previous move. One likely reason for the quick decision is that Bxe1 was a natural capture, while the other options either committed the pawns or left material hanging. With about 16 minutes left and a small clock lead, Sindarov may have also wanted to save time after two earlier thinks of over 15 minutes.

likely_reasons.reason: Bxe1 was a straightforward bishop capture, while the alternatives such as f7 and Kh4 were drastically worse according to the engine.
Gukesh's previous move 48...Kxf5 was a capture, so recapturing with Bxe1 was probably the natural reply.

narrative.headline: Sindarov finds the only saving bishop move quickly
narrative.text: In a sparse endgame, Sindarov played 58.Bd2 in just 10 seconds, and it was the engine's top choice, keeping the evaluation at an even 0.0. It was a true only-move position: the engine rated just one good move, and nearby bishop retreats like Bf2 or Bg3 would have allowed a forced mate against Sindarov. Gukesh had just played 57...Ke2 in only 5 seconds, so the game was moving at a brisk pace. With only six legal moves and two pieces left besides kings and pawns, Sindarov probably had few options to sort through, which may explain the quick decision despite the danger. One likely factor is the clock: Sindarov started the move about three minutes behind Gukesh, at 12m 59s. After an earlier game with long thinks of over 15 minutes on 16.b3 and 21.c3, Sindarov may have wanted to keep the pace up, finishing the move with 13m 19s.

likely_reasons.reason: With only six legal moves and very little material left, there were few candidate moves for Sindarov to weigh.
Gukesh's fast 57...Ke2 and Sindarov's three-minute clock deficit probably encouraged a quick reply.
